name: Natural Cycles
tagline: App-based fertility awareness that is cleared as a contraceptive, using daily basal body temperature and cycle data.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Annual billing is cheaper and a thermometer or wearable is usually required.

verdictSummary: The math is not the product. A sympto-thermal rule engine over logged temperatures and LH tests is genuinely a one-sitting build, and the algorithm family it descends from is public knowledge. What you cannot build is FDA clearance, a CE mark, published clinical effectiveness trials, and the legal standing to tell someone they can skip a condom tonight. Natural Cycles sells a regulated medical claim with a number attached to it, and a personal script sells you a chart you are grading yourself on. If you want a cycle log, build it. If you want contraception, this is the wrong aisle.
coreLoopDIY: A local app where you log daily basal body temperature, LH strips and cycle events, and it draws the chart and flags a probable fertile window using published sympto-thermal rules.
requirements: A basal thermometer with two-decimal resolution, used at the same time every morning
Months of consistent daily logging before any pattern is trustworthy
Willingness to read up on sympto-thermal rules yourself
Somewhere to run it that you actually open every morning
whatYouLose: Regulatory clearance: no FDA clearance, no CE mark, no validated effectiveness figure behind your green days
Clinical validation: their fertile-window algorithm has been through trials, yours has been through your own vibes
Device integrations: Bluetooth thermometer sync and wearable temperature data from Oura and friends
Mode switching: prevent, plan and pregnancy follow-through flows built around the same data
Someone to blame and ask: support, documentation, and an accountable company if the prediction is wrong
moatNotes: Contraceptive claims are regulated in most jurisdictions. A personal build can display the same numbers and legally promise nothing.
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay because the subscription is not for the chart, it is for the clearance. A regulated contraceptive claim means someone ran trials, published a failure rate, and carries the liability for the method. That is the entire reason anyone trusts a temperature curve enough to change their behaviour because of it, and no amount of local tooling reproduces it. The hardware pairing and the polished daily nudge matter too, but they are garnish on top of the paperwork.
notes: The chart is a weekend afternoon; the claim behind the chart is not. The moat is regulatory clearance plus clinical trial data, and no self-hosted app can issue itself either one.
prompt:
Build a local-only fertility and cycle tracking app for one person. This is a data logger and charting tool, NOT a contraceptive device, and it must say so loudly.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Python 3.12, FastAPI, Jinja2 templates, HTMX for interactions
- SQLite via SQLModel, file at ./data/cycles.db
- Chart.js from a vendored static file, no CDN at runtime
- uv for dependency management, single `uv run uvicorn app:app --reload` to start

Data model:
- DayEntry: date (unique), waking_temp_c (nullable, 2 decimals), temp_time, temp_quality enum (good, disturbed, skipped), cervical_mucus enum (dry, sticky, creamy, eggwhite, watery, none_observed), lh_test enum (not_taken, negative, positive), bleeding enum (none, spotting, light, medium, heavy), notes
- Cycle: derived, starts on first medium/heavy bleeding day after a non-bleeding day

Features in scope:
- One-screen daily log form, defaults to today, keyboard friendly, saves with HTMX without a full reload
- Cycle chart: temperature line with disturbed days marked differently, mucus and LH icons along the x axis, cycle day numbering
- A rules engine in rules.py implementing textbook sympto-thermal interpretation: three-over-six temperature rise detection, first positive LH, peak mucus day. Keep every rule in a named pure function with a docstring citing which rule it is.
- A clearly labelled "estimated fertile window" band, always rendered with its own confidence caveat and the rules that fired
- Cycle history table: length, luteal phase length, day of rise
- CSV export and CSV import of all entries
- A morning reminder is OUT of scope; instead print a one-line summary endpoint at /today.json you can wire to your own cron

Explicitly out of scope:
- Accounts, cloud sync, telemetry, analytics, any network call after install
- Bluetooth or wearable device integration
- Any string anywhere that implies contraceptive protection, safe days, or a failure rate

Safety copy requirement:
- Persistent banner on every page: this tool is a personal log, it is not a medical device and not birth control, and it has not been clinically validated
- Same text in the README, first paragraph

Config: read PORT and DB_PATH from .env via python-dotenv, ship .env.example, gitignore .env and ./data.
Write pytest tests for rules.py covering a textbook ovulatory cycle, an anovulatory cycle with no sustained rise, and a cycle with two disturbed days inside the rise window.
